sense: lay a burden, a task, a rule or a penalty on someone

terms.gloss: lay on, impose (a burden, a task, a law, a tax)
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation: the thing in the accusative, the person in the dative
evidence: Cic. Att. 13.11.1: nē magnum onus observantiae Brūtō nostrō impōnerem (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Phil. 7.15: lēgēs cīvitātī per vim imposuit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Literally to put on or into (a load on an animal, a pot on the fire); of burdens, tasks, laws, names and taxes the same. With a dative alone it also means to deceive: Catōnī ēgregiē imposuit Milō noster (Cic. Q. Fr. 2.6.5, Lewis & Short), “our Milo took Cato in beautifully”. So “I don’t want to impose on you” is not tibi impōnere: see impose on.

terms.gloss: lay on, enjoin (a task, a burden, a duty)
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation: the thing in the accusative, the person in the dative
terms.comment: Literally to join or fasten into; Lewis & Short gives impōnō as its synonym in this sense. Livy’s word, and Pliny’s for a task one is given.

phrases.latin: nē magnum onus observantiae Brūtō nostrō impōnerem
phrases.english: so as not to impose on our Brutus the great burden of attending on me
he imposed laws on the state by force
our Milo took Cato in beautifully (impōnere with a dative alone: deceive)

phrases.latin: Nōlī puerō plūs oneris impōnere quam ferre potest.
phrases.english: Don’t put more on the boy than he can carry.

sources: Lewis & Short: impono · Lewis & Short: injungo
